SEC13A-01.note: Second clause has a noun-clause subject ('how the animals tell ... remained uncertain'), so it is independent; comma + 'but' joins. B is a comma splice disguised because 'how' looks subordinating (strongest distractor). C 'though how' leaves a fragment after the semicolon. D 'in how' strikable at a glance. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct.

SEC13A-02.note: 'reveal [to anyone ... impressions] [how many ... apprentices]': postponed object after a long prepositional phrase; no punctuation between verb-phrase and its object. A (comma) is the strongest distractor since the long phrase invites a pause. C leaves 'reveal ...' without an object; D 'and how' likewise objectless. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct, incl. D reading as second object of 'with'.

SEC13A-03.note: After the blank: fronted 'until ... 1870s,' then main clause 'photographers ... had to carry'. Needs a coordinator: ', so'. A is a comma splice (strongest, as 'until' reads as subordinating the whole); B same plus attaches 'until' to 'dried'; D 'even' is not a conjunction. Only C has a FANBOYS, which a test-wise student may spot. PHASE 2: Key matches. Note A-03 shares the wet-collodion photography topic with B-03 (near-duplicate stimulus content in one batch).

SEC13A-04.note: Dash opened after 'revealed' must be closed by a dash. Once the opening dash is spotted, all three others fall by the paired-punctuation rule. A (comma) strongest because the interrupter itself contains commas. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct. Free by dash-pair spotting; medium, not hard.

SEC13A-05.note: 'the notebooks make one pattern unmistakable' is complete; what follows is a full clause specifying the pattern: colon. A comma splice; C splices later at 'survives, the hives' while making 'in nearly every season' attach to 'unmistakable' (strongest); D 'which in ... the hives gained' ungrammatical. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct.

SEC13A-06.note: Fronted 'Beside several of the deeper prints, in mud ...,' then 'they identified' = new independent clause; semicolon. A splice; B (no comma) attaches 'beside' to 'meters' and still splices at 'burial, they' (strongest); D 'beside which ... they identified' broken relative. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct.

SEC13B-01.note: Subject 'The fossil teeth that ... dug from an eroding riverbank over a single wet summer' -> verb 'settled'; no punctuation inside the restrictive clause or between subject and verb. A (dash) strongest because the earlier dash pair primes another dash, but that pair is already closed. B 'which' makes the riverbank the settler and orphans the subject; C single comma splits subject from verb. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct.

SEC13B-02.note: Semicolon already precedes 'when'; the nonrestrictive 'whose livers ... fragments' needs a closing comma, and 'however' then interrupts the main clause 'the ... effect vanished'. A (semicolon before however) is the reflex answer and strongest distractor, but leaves the when-clause as a fragment. B same with period; D puts the clause break after 'however', leaving a fragment. Genuinely hard. PHASE 2: Key matches. Best item in the batch.

SEC13B-03.note: Closing dash after 'poisoning' requires an opening dash before the appositive 'three chemicals...'. Spotting the later dash kills all three distractors. C (comma) strongest since it would be fine without the closing dash. PHASE 2: Key matches. Same topic as A-03. Free by dash-pair spotting; medium.

SEC13B-04.note: Inverted 'did they leave' plus question mark mark a direct question, which must start its own sentence. B (comma splice into a direct question) strongest; C and D fall by the question mark / inversion at a glance (D's indirect question cannot invert). PHASE 2: Key matches, explanation correct, but the closing question mark plus inversion makes it easy; author's 'hard' label is wrong. Off-route for module-2 hard: drop or re-band to easy/medium.

SEC13B-05.note: 'rapidly gathers' needs a subject; only 'that' (relative pronoun for 'protein') supplies one, with 'in the presence of ... tear' as an unpunctuated interrupter. B, C, D all leave 'gathers' subjectless; C/D strongest because 'the presence of the calcium ions admitted through a tear' can be misread as a subject or the clause looks complete. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation for B ('and gathers' cannot agree with 'researchers'/'identified') is sound.

SEC13B-06.note: Appositive 'a former apprentice ... quit the workshop' opened by a comma after 'printer' must close with a comma before the direct object 'the exclusive right'. B (dash) strongest; A period leaves 'granted the printer, ...' and a fragment; C no closure. PHASE 2: Key matches. Explanation correct; comma-pair matching, medium.
